He was, in fact, arrayed as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” among his most extraordinary impersonations. The Cantervilles had excellent cause to remember it, for it had truly occasioned their dispute with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. The time was roughly a quarter past two in the morning, and so far as he could discover, nobody was about. Yet as he sauntered towards the library to inspect what remained of the blood-stain, two figures suddenly sprang upon him from a shadowy corner, flinging their arms wildly above their heads and shrieking “BOO!” into his ear.

Overcome by a panic entirely natural in the circumstances, he dashed towards the stairs, only to encounter Washington Otis waiting there with the large garden-syringe. Thus surrounded by foes and almost brought to bay, he disappeared into the great iron stove, mercifully unlit, and was obliged to return home by the flues and chimneys. He reached his chamber in a dreadful condition of filth, confusion, and despair.

Afterwards he was never observed upon another nightly expedition. Several times the twins waited in ambush, and every night they scattered nutshells along the corridors, greatly vexing both parents and servants; but their efforts were fruitless. Evidently his feelings had suffered too deeply to permit his appearance. Mr. Otis accordingly returned to his extensive history of the Democratic Party, a labour already occupying several years. Mrs. Otis arranged an admirable clam-bake which astonished the entire county. The boys turned to lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national pastimes; while Virginia rode her pony through the lanes beside the young Duke of Cheshire, who had arrived to pass the final week of his holidays at Canterville Chase. The general belief was that the ghost had departed. Indeed, Mr. Otis wrote as much to Lord Canterville, whose answer conveyed his great satisfaction and offered hearty congratulations to the Minister's estimable wife.

The Otises were mistaken, however. The ghost remained within the house and, though now little better than an invalid, had no intention of abandoning the affair. He was particularly unwilling after learning that the visitors included the young Duke of Cheshire. The Duke's grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would throw dice with the Canterville ghost. Next morning he was discovered upon the card-room floor, so helplessly paralysed that, although he survived to an advanced age, he could never afterwards utter anything except “Double Sixes.”

But I wonder how much longer you would have continued if left to yourself. When would you have spoken, I wonder, had I not questioned you? My determination to thank you for your goodness to Lydia certainly accomplished a great deal. Too great a deal, I fear; for where is the moral if our happiness arises from a broken promise, since I ought never to have raised the matter? That will never answer.”

“You need feel no concern. The moral will remain entirely proper. Lady Catherine's indefensible attempts to part us dispelled every doubt I had. Your eagerness to declare your gratitude is not responsible for my present happiness. I was in no disposition to wait until you offered an opportunity. My aunt's report had encouraged me, and I meant to discover the whole truth immediately.”

“Lady Catherine has proved infinitely useful, which should delight her, since usefulness is her passion. But tell me why you came to Netherfield. Was your only purpose to ride over to Longbourn and feel awkward, or did you contemplate more important results?”

“My actual object was to see you and determine, if possible, whether I could ever hope to win your affection. The object I professed, at least to myself, was to discover whether your sister retained her regard for Bingley, and, if so, to make the confession I have since made to him.”

“Will you ever summon the courage to inform Lady Catherine of what awaits her?”

“Time is more likely to fail me than courage, Elizabeth. Still, it must be done. Give me a sheet of paper, and I shall do it at once.”

“If I had no letter of my own to write, I could sit beside you and praise the regularity of your handwriting, as another young lady once did. But I, too, possess an aunt who must no longer be neglected.”

Reluctant to admit how greatly Mrs. Gardiner had exaggerated her intimacy with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth had not yet answered her aunt's long letter. Now, with news she knew would be warmly welcomed, she was almost ashamed that her uncle and aunt had already been deprived of three happy days, and immediately wrote:

“My dear aunt, I ought long ago to have thanked you for your kind, lengthy, and satisfying account of all the particulars. The truth is that I was too cross to write. You imagined more than existed. But now imagine whatever you please. Let your fancy range freely; allow your imagination every possible flight the subject invites. Unless you suppose me already married, you cannot go far wrong.

Does not comprehend English, but bases his judgment upon the tone.

“Alberto Montani, confectioner, states that he was one of the earliest to go upstairs. Heard the voices mentioned. The harsh voice belonged to a Frenchman; several words were intelligible. The man seemed to be remonstrating. Could distinguish none of the high-pitched speaker's words. Utterance rapid and irregular. Believes the voice Russian. Confirms the testimony in general. Is himself Italian and has never spoken with a Russian native.

“Several witnesses, questioned again, declared that every chimney on the fourth floor was too narrow to allow a human body through. The term ‘sweeps’ referred to cylindrical brushes of the sort used in chimney-cleaning. Such brushes had been worked up and down every flue throughout the house. No rear passage exists by which anyone might have gone down while the party climbed the stairs. Mademoiselle L'Espanaye's body was wedged so tightly in the chimney that four or five persons had to combine their strength before they could pull it free.

“Paul Dumas, physician, states that he was summoned about dawn to inspect the bodies. Both then lay upon the bedstead's sacking in the room where Mademoiselle L. had been discovered. The young lady's corpse bore extensive bruises and abrasions, sufficiently explained by its having been forced up the chimney. Her throat was severely rubbed. Beneath the chin were several deep scratches and a succession of dark marks plainly made by fingers. The face was dreadfully discoloured, the eyeballs projecting, and the tongue partly bitten through. A considerable bruise at the pit of the stomach appeared to have resulted from the pressure of a knee. M. Dumas believed Mademoiselle L'Espanaye had been strangled by an unknown person or persons. The mother's remains were frightfully mutilated. Every bone of the right arm and leg was shattered to some extent. The left tibia and all the ribs on that side were badly splintered. The entire body showed terrible bruising and discoloration. The means of inflicting these injuries could not be determined. A heavy wooden club, a broad iron bar, a chair, or any large, weighty, blunt instrument could have caused them if handled by a man of exceptional strength. No woman, whatever her weapon, could have delivered such blows. When examined by the witness, the deceased's head was completely detached and itself severely broken. The throat had plainly been severed with an exceedingly sharp implement, most probably a razor.
